Many pathogens are known to be transmitted sexually including: • bacteria: • Chlamydia trachomatis (see Lymphogranuloma Venereum, p.192 and Chlamydial Infections, p.166) • Haemophilus ducreyi (see Chancroid, p.191) • Klebsiella granulomatis (see Granuloma Inguinale, p.192) • Neisseria gonorrhoeae (see Gonorrhoea, p.191) • Treponema pallidum (see Syphilis, p.192) • Ureaplasma urealyticum • protozoa: • Trichomonas vaginalis (see Trichomoniasis, p.827). • viruses: • human immunodeficiency virus (see HIV Infection and AIDS, p.856) • hepatitis viruses (see Hepatitis, p.851) • herpesviruses (see Herpesvirus Infections, p.853) Clinical syndromes associated with sexually transmitted diseases, and which are discussed in this section, include urethritis (p.199) and epididymitis (p.170) in men; cervici- tis (p.166), pelvic inflammatory disease (p.184), and bac- terial vaginosis (p.164) in women; and proctitis (p.188). Perinatal transmission of sexually transmitted pathogens from the mother can result in neonatal conjunctivitis (p.180) or pneumonia (p.186). General guidelines for the management of sexually trans- mitted diseases have been published1-3 although recom- mendations may need to be localised because of differenc- es in patterns of infection and drug resistance. Early detection and treatment are required to prevent long-term complications, including infertility, still-births and neona- tal infections, genital cancers, and an increased risk of ac- quiring and transmitting HIV. The suggestion that spermicidal contraceptives may pro- vide some protection against sexually transmitted diseases is discussed under Nonoxinols, p.1917. 1. CDC.
